title: What the homepage has to prove for an education product
metaTitle: Education product homepage: the lesson first
excerpt: Show the learning moment and a way to start a class or a trial. A dashboard full of badges reassures the team and confuses a teacher or a parent.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights, a clear display the way a lesson should be the first thing in view.
caption: Folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an education homepage show first?
faqs.answer: The learning moment: the exercise, the hint, or the teacher view of who is stuck, plus a way to start a class or a trial. A badge wall, a mission statement, and a stock photo of children pointing at a blank screen do not answer a parent or a teacher.

faqs.question: Can one homepage serve both teachers and parents?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the first screen is the same honest lesson and the next block gives each a short path. The signups should stay distinct. A teacher who needs a class and a parent who needs one child should not be forced through the same vague button.

faqs.question: What should the page refuse?
faqs.answer: Fear-based headlines, invented learning gains, and a cinematic product you do not ship. Match the first screen to the trial. The buyer will open the product immediately after, and the two have to agree.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
An education product homepage has one job for a teacher or a parent with little time: show the learning moment, and offer a way to start a class or a trial. The product is a lesson, a practice, or a class. The page has to look like that.

A dashboard full of badges fails this buyer. Streaks, points, and leaderboards reassure the team that the product feels alive. They do not tell a parent whether a child will learn the skill, or a teacher whether the activity fits the period they actually have.

## Show the learning moment first

The learning moment is a specific scene. A child reads a sentence and tries the next one. A student works a step and sees why it was wrong without a cartoon scolding them. A teacher glances at a list and sees which three students are stuck on the same idea. Pick the scene your product truly does. Put it on the first screen, in a sentence and in the product itself.

Write the sentence as the lesson, not as the company. "Ten quiet minutes of reading practice a parent can start tonight" is a learning moment. "Reimagining the future of learning" is a billboard. The teacher who opens your tab between classes, and the parent who opens it after bedtime, do not have time for the billboard. [Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a page has to make its value clear in about 10 seconds to earn a longer look. They also read only about a quarter of the text. Your quarter is the moment and the way to begin.

Show the product doing the thing. A real screen, cropped to the exercise or the teacher's view, beats an illustration of a smiling child pointing at a generic tablet. If the screen is still ugly, fix the screen that is the product. Do not hide it under a marketing collage. Buyers of education tools have been shown collages. They scroll until they see whether there is a lesson.

Name the learner and the setting in the first lines. Early reading at home. Fractions in a middle-school period. A tutor session in a noisy afternoon. If you serve more than one, lead with the one you want next, and give the other a plain path. A hero that tries to be a school, a family, and a district explains none of them.

## Why a badge dashboard fails

Badges fail because they answer the team's question, not the buyer's. The team asks whether people come back. The parent asks whether the child is learning to read. The teacher asks whether this replaces a worksheet or adds one. A wall of streaks, XP, and ranks makes the product look like a game about the product. The learning is somewhere underneath, if it is there at all.

You can still use encouragement inside the product. A quiet "that's the idea" after a hard step can be humane. A public leaderboard on the homepage is a different choice. It tells a cautious parent that comparison is the point. It tells a teacher that the loudest students will be the story. If that is not your pedagogy, do not let the marketing page invent one.

Replace the badge wall with one completed moment and one next step. Show a problem, the learner's move, and what the product does next. If you have a teacher view, show the three-line summary they would check while walking the room, not the analytics atrium you built for a demo day. Demo-day screens are how education sites start lying. The buyer who lives in the classroom can tell.

If your real retention story is good, put it where a skeptic can interpret it. "Students who finish the ten-minute practice four days in a week" needs a source and a plain definition, and it still should not lead. The moment leads. The number, if you may publish it and it is true, supports. Do not invent a gain. A false learning statistic is worse than no statistic. Teachers repeat numbers. They will not forgive a made-up one.

## Two readers, one page

A teacher and a parent do not want the same second paragraph. They can share the first screen if the learning moment is honest. Under it, give each a short path.

For a teacher: what the activity covers, how long it takes, what they still have to do, and how a class or a trial starts. Mention the practical constraints without drama. A finite period. A roster. A projector or a cart of aging laptops. If the product assumes one child and a quiet room, say so, and do not dress it up as a whole-class system.

For a parent: what the child does, how long it takes, what it costs to try, and what the parent is not expected to teach. Parents are often afraid the product will hand them a lesson plan. If it does not, say that. If it does, say that too. Surprise is how trials get abandoned on a weeknight.

Do not build two visual languages. Same type, same product frames, two short columns or two stacked blocks. The page should feel like one product with two doors, not like a company that could not decide. A navigation label for teachers and one for families can do the rest. The homepage's job is to prove the moment and offer the start.

Write at a reading level a tired adult can parse. Short sentences. The skill in ordinary words. "Addition with regrouping" is clearer than "numeracy outcomes." Save framework names for the page where a curriculum lead asked for them. The homepage is for the person who might start a class or a trial today.

## A way to start a class or a trial

The action should say which beginning this is. Start a class. Start a trial. If both exist, they need two honest labels, not one button called "Get started" that dumps everyone into the same vague signup. A teacher who needs a roster and a parent who needs a single child are not the same signup. Pretending they are is how you collect the wrong account and a support ticket.

Say what the trial includes and when it ends. A week of the real lesson, not a tour of locked units. No card if that is true. A card later, stated now, if that is true. Hidden billing is a betrayal in this category, because the buyer is often spending school trust or household money, not a software hobby budget.

Say what they will have at the end of the first session. A teacher will have run one activity and seen who was stuck. A parent will have finished one short practice and know whether the child stayed with it. That promise should be small enough to be true on day one. Grand outcomes ("close the gap") do not belong on the button. They belong, carefully and without fake numbers, nowhere near the button.

Put the action on the first screen and again after the proof. Repeat the same words. Do not introduce "Book a demo" as a third verb unless a demo is actually how schools buy, and then label it for schools. A parent who hits a demo form will leave. A district buyer who hits a consumer trial may also leave. The words are the routing.

## How little time you have

Design the first screen as if the tab will be closed when the bell rings. Headline in two or three lines. One product frame. One action. A single line that says who it is for. Everything else can wait below, and most of it should be cut.

The title in the browser can carry the plain description. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for a concise, descriptive title that belongs to this page. Let the on-page heading be the learning moment. Let the title say what the product teaches and for whom. Do not paste a slogan into both and add the skill as an afterthought.

Below the fold, answer the next three questions and stop. What does a session look like? What do you need to begin? What does it cost to try, even if the full pricing page holds the detail? A long essay on your philosophy of childhood will not be read. A short paragraph on what you refuse, such as public leaderboards or ads inside the lesson, will be read, because it is a safety check.

Proof sits under that, still brief. One classroom or one family story, with the constraint and the decision, not a carousel of unnamed stars. If you cannot publish a story yet, publish the lesson itself. The product is allowed to be the proof. A quote you cannot verify is not.

## What the homepage should refuse

Refuse the badge dashboard, the stock photo of diverse children in a circle with no lesson in frame, the logo parade of schools that are not customers, and the mission statement before the exercise. Refuse "AI-powered" as the headline unless the learning moment is impossible to understand without that fact. Most buyers want the lesson. The machinery can be a later sentence.

Refuse guilt. "Don't let your child fall behind" is a common education-page mistake. It spends the first screen on fear. Fear is not a learning moment. Show the work the child or the class will do. Adults can decide if it matters. You do not need to threaten them.

Refuse a different product than the one you ship. If the live product is a plain practice screen, do not market a cinematic world you hope to build. The trial will be the audit. Match the page to the build. Hanabi designs and builds the page and the interface as one thing when that is the engagement, so the marketing frame and the product frame do not drift apart. Whatever your setup, the homepage should be able to survive a buyer who opens the app immediately after.

Keep the stack talk off this page. Fast, readable, and usable on a phone is the promise. The framework is not the headline.

## After the first screen

Read the page on a phone in one sitting, as a parent, then again as a teacher. Each time, stop at ten seconds and say what the learner does and how you would start. If you talk about badges, culture, or the founding story, rewrite the first screen. Do not add a section. Replace the one that failed.

When the moment is clear, the next question is what it costs and what is included. [A pricing page for an education product](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-an-education-product) is the page to write next. A teacher or a parent uses it to judge fit, not to do arithmetic, and they will ask what a class or a trial includes even if you hoped to save that for a call.

If you want a studio to shape the first screen around the lesson rather than the badge wall, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Read those projects for the decision on the first screen. Then ask whether your homepage shows a learner learning, or a company celebrating a dashboard.
